_source.file: Master of the Seven Seas — Fleet Roster
_source.note: Sean's own revision of the fleet roster, read from Drive and imported verbatim. It supersedes the v2.4 JSON export of the same day: twenty-four hulls now rather than twenty-five, four starting ships and eight research unlocks a side, and the Confederacy's gapped ladder closed. Combat resolution is not here and never was — that is the 7 Seas — Naval Combat System document. Change this file by re-reading the sheet, not by hand.

_notes.note: The name collides with a legend hull in the live game: the Ironback is the Crown dreadnought Admiral Dorian Jessup took with him when he left the Imperium's service, and she is named in his fleet-command power. Sean's ruling of 18 September was to keep the legend and rename the roster ship, which is where the provisional 'Frostback' came from. This revision of the roster, written by him afterwards, says Ironback — so Ironback it is here, imported as written. Nothing reads this name but a label, and the collision is recorded rather than resolved.

Dreadnought (now Morningstar), Long-Gun Line Ship, Wayfinder II, Freebooter, Swallowtail (which the v2.4 import had renamed Bonecutter for the same legend-hull reason), Reefwalker (now Reefwarden) and Reef-Class (now Coral-Class Dreadnaught). The Swallowtail collision is gone with the ship: she belongs to Reyne again.

purpose.Purpose: Authoritative working roster for ship progression, strategic roles, tier placement, construction economics, and faction identity. Combat-resolution rules remain defined in the separate Naval Combat System document.
purpose.Roster structure: Each faction has four starting ships and eight research unlocks. Research order establishes progression, not strict replacement: efficient, specialized, and logistical ships may remain useful throughout the campaign.
purpose.Faction contrast: The Crown favors standardized progression, disciplined combined fleets, and increasingly dominant capital ships. The Confederacy favors asymmetric specialists, retrofits, raiders, living-coral vessels, and ships that combine military and strategic utility.
purpose.Balance philosophy: Every ship should have a clear reason to build it and an intentional weakness. Power may be paid for through cost, construction time, upkeep, speed, repair, fragility, narrow specialization, or dependence on fleet support.
purpose.Current status: Ship concepts and tier identities are approved working designs. Exact numerical balance remains subject to simulation and playtesting; future revisions should preserve each ship's defining role and tradeoffs.

designRules.Early-game power: Starting ships may be strong, but multiple high-tier capabilities require major drawbacks such as poor efficiency, fragility, Slow speed, weak repair, or narrow specialization.
designRules.Fleet structure: Each faction fields four starting ships followed by eight research unlocks. New research should expand fleet-building choices rather than make every earlier hull obsolete.
designRules.Crown doctrine: Standardized combined-arms fleets, dependable progression, strong Heavy Guns and capital ships, and deliberate reliance on escorts to cover specialist weaknesses.
designRules.Confederacy doctrine: Asymmetric specialists, fast raiders, retrofits, amphibious reef technology, regeneration, and ships that trade standardization for unusual strategic advantages.
designRules.Weapon system: The roster uses Long Guns, Heavy Guns, and Light Guns. Gun tiers describe battery strength; ships should not receive every category unless broad armament is central to their identity.
designRules.Long Guns: A midgame technology milestone used primarily for retreat fire and pursuit. Long Guns do not grant First Strike in normal combat.
designRules.Bombardment: A strategic siege rating used against fortifications and locations. It never contributes to ship-to-ship damage; specialized ordnance may justify Bombardment without naval Heavy or Long Guns.
designRules.Value and specialization: Ships are not expected to offer equal general value. Some may be deliberate value monsters, while inefficient ships remain desirable because they provide a scarce capability. Every ship still needs a clear strategic reason to build it, and extreme strengths should carry visible tradeoffs.
designRules.Maintenance baseline: Standard daily maintenance is ceil(Gold to Build × 1%). Efficient ships fall below this rate; inefficient, cheap, improvised, or difficult-to-service ships may exceed it substantially.
designRules.Build-time baseline: On-rate construction has Days to Build equal to Gold to Build. Faster or slower completion is an intentional production advantage or drawback; the overall range runs from roughly 40 days to 1,000 days for Majestic.
designRules.Gun-cost baseline: On-rate armament value is (Long Guns + Heavy Guns + Light Guns) × 50 gold. A ship costing more allocates value to defense, speed, utility, regeneration, or another capability; a ship costing less receives above-rate firepower and must pay elsewhere.
designRules.Endgame: Majestic remains the strongest individual ship. Urskin Whaler supplies the Confederacy's greatest hull, troop capacity, and Heavy Gun mass; the Coral-Class Dreadnaught supplies regenerative, heavily armored combined-arms power. Together they exceed a lone Majestic.

ships.Design Notes: Low-threat strategic transport with T1 Light Guns, T2 Hull, and capacity for four troops. Its modest combat profile reduces its targeting priority, helping it preserve valuable embarked forces.
Very Fast and inexpensive, with T2 Light Guns but no Armor and only T1 Hull. Individually fragile; dangerous when fielded in numbers against lightly protected Confederate ships.

An intentionally inefficient but powerful starting warship. T3 Heavy Guns, Armor, Hull, and Bombardment deliver strong early damage, offset by Slow speed, poor repair, high construction cost, and exceptional upkeep.
The Crown's starting capital ship combines strong Heavy Guns, Armor, Hull, Bombardment, and troop capacity. Its limited Light Guns leave it vulnerable to fast swarms unless screened by Interceptors.

An efficiency upgrade over Morningstar: Normal speed, lower construction and maintenance costs, and strong repair. It sacrifices some Heavy Guns, Armor, and Bombardment for better overall fleet value.

Replaces Interceptor I as the Crown's fast workhorse. T2 Light Guns, T1 Heavy Guns, light Armor, T1 Bombardment, and one troop give it broad utility; rapid construction is balanced by inefficient upkeep.
Introduces Crown Long Guns. T2 Long and Heavy Guns, T2 Armor, T3 Hull, and three troops make it a durable fleet anchor. No Light Guns and poor repair require dedicated screening support.
Improves Vanguard with greater Armor, Hull, and Heavy Gun strength while retaining exceptional repair efficiency. A durable, cost-effective core ship for mature Crown fleets.
A dramatic Interceptor upgrade: Very Fast, T3 Long Guns, T4 Light Guns, and T2 Armor. Its T1 Hull, high price, and costly upkeep prevent it from trading efficiently in prolonged battles.
A purpose-built offensive warship with T3 Long, Heavy, and Light Guns, medium Armor, low-T3 Hull, and T2 Bombardment. No troop capacity; its value lies entirely in naval aggression.

A major Sovereign improvement with Normal speed, T4 Heavy Guns and Bombardment, stronger Armor, greater troop capacity, and only moderately increased upkeep. Reduced Light Guns preserve its need for escorts.

The strongest individual ship in the game. It combines top-tier weapons, Armor, Hull, Bombardment, and troop capacity; enormous cost, 1,000-day construction, high upkeep, and Slow speed limit its availability.
An extremely cheap, Very Fast exploration craft with no combat, transport, Armor, or bombardment capability. Its sole purpose is rapid reconnaissance and map control.

A former merchant brigantine retrofitted with T1 Light Guns. Fast, inexpensive, and able to carry two troops, it retains a sturdy T2 commercial hull but lacks Armor and dedicated naval or siege weapons.

A Slow warship assembled from mismatched hull sections, salvaged Armor, and improvised weapons. T2 Armor and strong T2 Hull make it difficult to sink, while sub-rate guns, poor repair, and inefficient upkeep reflect its retrofit construction.

A living-coral starting warship grown by the amphibious reef peoples. T2 Light Guns, T1 Armor, T2 Hull, and exceptional regeneration make it a sustainable early combatant rather than a burst-damage vessel.

A Fast, mass-efficient raider with T3 Light Guns, two troops, and T1 Bombardment from specialized raiding ordnance. No Armor and T1 Hull make it vulnerable, but its speed and versatility enable independent coastal attacks.
The Confederacy's first conventional fleet warship. Normal speed, Heavy Guns, supporting Light Guns, and Armor focus it on naval combat; it carries no troops and contributes no Bombardment.
Introduces Confederate Long Guns. Fast speed, T2 Long Guns and Armor, T1 Heavy and Light Guns, three troops, and T2 Bombardment create a highly mobile assault platform with broad strategic utility.

Purpose-built to close the Confederacy's Heavy Gun gap and challenge major Imperium warships. T3 Heavy Guns, T2 Light Guns, T3 Armor, T2 Hull, and four troops; no Long Guns or Bombardment. High cost and long construction are offset by low upkeep.
A dedicated siege platform with T4 Long Guns and Bombardment. T3 Armor and Hull discourage enemy targeting, while T1 Heavy Guns, no Light Guns, no troops, and poor repair keep it specialized.
A Fast, maneuverable specialist carrying the game's only T4 Light Gun battery. It has no troops, Heavy Guns, Long Guns, or Bombardment; efficient cost and rapid construction support mass deployment.

The largest hull in the game and a nine-troop invasion platform. T4 Heavy Guns, T3 Long Guns, Armor, and Bombardment deliver enormous strategic weight; Slow speed, no Light Guns, and standard-rate upkeep define its limits.

The final Confederate capital ship. T4+ Armor, T3 Hull, every gun category at T3, T3 Bombardment, Normal speed, and exceptional regeneration provide outstanding long-term value. Its 2,200-gold cost and 900-day growth cycle make deployment a major commitment.
